method: Entry-by-entry audit of citation, design, direction and magnitude against the auditing model's recalled knowledge of the published literature. No primary source was read: this container's network policy refuses every journal, DOI resolver and preprint host. Recall is not verification, and no entry here is tiered above the recall band.

culture:collectivist_conformity.note: Bond & Smith (1996, Psychological Bulletin) is the Asch line-judgment meta-analysis (133 studies, 17 countries, so n_cultures=17 matches) and did find collectivism predicted greater conformity; the multiplier and participant count are not theirs. | 'Conformity ~30% higher' / adjustment_factor 1.3 is a re-parameterization, not a published number; Bond & Smith reported a correlation between collectivism and conformity effect size (r in the .4 range), not a percentage multiplier; n_participants=25000 is not a figure I can attribute to the meta-analysis

culture:collectivist_cooperation.note: Balliet et al. (2014, Psychological Bulletin) is real and about ingroup favoritism in cooperation, but it is the wrong source for a culture-level adjustment factor, and the note's outgroup-derogation framing runs against the paper's ingroup-love conclusion. | Balliet, Wu & De Dreu (2014) is a meta-analysis of INGROUP FAVORITISM in cooperation (overall d ~0.32), not of collectivist-vs-individualist culture; using it to license a 1.2x collectivist multiplier attaches the citation to a claim it does not make; Their conclusion is that favoritism is driven by ingroup love rather than outgroup derogation, so 'outgroup discrimination also higher' misstates the finding; As I recall it, individualism-collectivism was not a strong moderator in that meta-analysis

corrected.notes: Ultimatum-game offers across the 15 small-scale societies ranged from ~26% mean (Machiguenga, modal 15%) to hyper-fair ~58% (Lamalera); dictator-game means across the 15 populations in Henrich et al. (2010, Science) averaged ~37%. Market integration positively predicted offers.
corrected.notes_was:
"Offers range from 15% (Machiguenga) to 58% (Lamelara). "
              "Market integration correlates with higher offers (r = 0.50)."

culture:dictator_giving_cross_cultural.note: Henrich et al. (2005 BBS 'Economic man in cross-cultural perspective') is the 15-society UG/PG paper; the cross-society DICTATOR data are Henrich et al. (2010, Science). The entry mixes the two. | The 15%-58% range is the Henrich et al. (2005, BBS) ULTIMATUM game, not dictator giving; construct label and numbers are from different paradigms; Machiguenga mean UG offer was ~26% (15% was the mode); 'Lamelara' misspelled; the society is Lamalera; r = 0.50 for market integration is not a figure I can place in either paper

corrected.notes: Dictator-game offers across the 15 populations averaged ~37% of the pie, with market-integrated populations at the high end; means above 50% were the exception, not the norm.
corrected.notes_was: Mean giving 50%+ in market-integrated small-scale societies.
corrected.source: Henrich et al. (2010, Science) — markets, religion, community size and the evolution of fairness

culture:dictator_giving_small_scale.note: The 2005 BBS paper ran ultimatum and public-goods/punishment games; the 15-society dictator-game data come from Henrich et al. (2010, Science), where DG means centered near 37%, not above 50%. | The cross-society DICTATOR game data are Henrich et al. (2010, Science), not the 2005 BBS paper (which ran ultimatum and third-party-punishment games); 'Mean giving 50%+' overstates it; DG means across those populations centered near 37%; adjustment_factor 1.5 applied to a ~28% Engel (2011) Western baseline yields ~42%, which is above the ~37% figure I recall

culture:east_asian_response_style.note: Chen, Lee & Stevenson (1995, Psychological Science) does document East Asian midpoint preference and North American extreme responding, and Heine et al. (2002, JPSP) the reference-group effect, so the direction is right; the specific multipliers and sample counts I cannot place. | adjustment_factor 0.85 / adjustment_additive -0.3 are engineering parameters, not published quantities; n_cultures=5 and n_participants=8000 do not correspond to either cited study (Chen et al. 1995 was a student sample in the low hundreds across US/Japan/Taiwan); Heine et al. (2002) is the reference-group-effect paper; it supports attenuated cross-cultural self-report differences, not an extremity multiplier

culture:east_asian_self_esteem.note: Schmitt & Allik (2005, JPSP) administered the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale in 53 nations and East Asian samples (Japan lowest) did score below Western ones, so the direction and the 4-point item format are right; the magnitude I cannot confirm from recall. | adjustment_factor 0.85 and the -0.5-point additive are not quantities I can attribute to Schmitt & Allik (2005); The RSES in that study is scored 1-4 per item but usually reported as a 10-item total, so a '0.5 points on 4-pt scale' shift is a per-item re-expression, not a published figure

culture:east_asian_social_desirability.note: The direction matches Lalwani, Shavitt & Johnson (2006, JPSP): impression management is higher under collectivist orientation. The 1.1 factor itself is not a published quantity. | adjustment_factor 1.1 is an engineering parameter; Lalwani et al. report standardized associations, not a 10% multiplier

corrected.notes: Baseline. Lalwani et al. (2006) found individualists higher on self-deceptive enhancement and collectivists higher on impression management, so the SELF-DECEPTION component is not culture-invariant.
corrected.notes_was: Baseline. Self-deception component similar across cultures.

culture:individualist_social_desirabilit.note: Lalwani, Shavitt & Johnson (2006, JPSP) dissociate the two Paulhus BIDR components by cultural orientation; the entry's note erases exactly the distinction the paper is about. | The note 'Self-deception component similar across cultures' contradicts Lalwani, Shavitt & Johnson (2006), whose central result is that individualism predicts self-deceptive enhancement while collectivism predicts impression management

culture:latin_american_response_style.note: Marin, Gamba & Marin (1992, JCCP) on Hispanic extreme responding and acquiescence, and Johnson, Kulesa, Cho & Shavitt (2005, JCCP, 19 countries) support the direction (acquiescence negatively related to individualism, ERS positively to power distance). The 1.15 multiplier is not theirs. | adjustment_factor 1.15 is an engineering parameter, not a published effect; n_participants=5000 does not match Johnson et al. (2005), which analyzed 19 countries of employee survey data, nor Marin et al.'s Hispanic samples

corrected.notes: MTurk data quality declined after ~2018 (Chmielewski & Kucker 2020). Note that Hauser & Schwarz (2016) found the opposite for the earlier era: MTurk workers passed attention checks MORE often than student subject-pool participants.
corrected.notes_was: MTurk data quality declining over time. More satisficing.
corrected.source: Chmielewski & Kucker (2020)

culture:mturk_response_quality.note: Chmielewski & Kucker (2020, SPPS) does document a post-2018 MTurk quality drop, but pairing it with Hauser & Schwarz (2016) as joint support is a citation-to-wrong-finding error. | Hauser & Schwarz (2016, Behavior Research Methods) 'Attentive Turkers' reports that MTurk participants were MORE attentive than subject-pool participants — it contradicts the entry's 'declining quality, more satisficing' claim rather than supporting it; adjustment_factor 0.95 is an engineering parameter with no published counterpart

corrected.notes: Peterson (2001) found student responses slightly MORE homogeneous than nonstudent responses, and student-derived effect sizes frequently differed from nonstudent ones both in magnitude AND in direction — not a uniform attenuation.
corrected.notes_was: Student samples show ~10% smaller effects than non-student in consumer studies.

culture:student_vs_nonstudent.note: Peterson (2001, Journal of Consumer Research 28(3), 450-461; 30 meta-analyses, 65 relationships) reported greater response homogeneity for students and effect sizes differing directionally as well as in magnitude. Hanel & Vione (2016, PLOS ONE) likewise reports difference, not attenuation. | '~10% smaller effects' is not Peterson's conclusion; his second-order meta-analysis emphasized directional reversals and heterogeneity, so a single 0.9 multiplier misrepresents the result; adjustment_factor 0.9 is therefore not a published quantity, and the sign of the student-nonstudent difference is not fixed

culture:western_baseline.note: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) 'The weirdest people in the world?' (BBS) is the standard WEIRD-critique citation, and this row is a definitional all-zero baseline making no numeric claim, so there is nothing to be wrong.

corrected.notes: Bimodal: dropout (bid 0) vs aggressive overbidding. Aggregate expenditure EXCEEDS the Nash prediction (over-dissipation).
corrected.notes_was: Bimodal: dropout (bid 0) vs overbidding. Aggregate near Nash.

game:all_pay_auction_standard.note: Dechenaux, Kovenock & Sheremeta (2015, Exp Econ) survey: all-pay auctions and contests show systematic over-dissipation; bimodality (dropouts vs overbidders) is correctly noted. | 'Aggregate near Nash' contradicts the over-dissipation regularity in the contest literature

corrected.notes: ~55% choose their own preferred equilibrium; without communication miscoordination is frequent (often 40-60% of pairs). Focal points and communication raise coordination.
corrected.notes_was: ~55% choose own preferred equilibrium. Miscoordination ~15%. Focal points help.

game:battle_of_sexes_standard.note: Cooper, DeJong, Forsythe & Ross (1989, RAND J Econ) is the right battle-of-sexes communication study; the entry's own fields disagree on the mean and understate miscoordination. | mean_proportion=0.50 contradicts the note and the subpopulation vector, both of which say 0.55 chose own-preferred; miscoordination=0.15 is far too low for the uncommunicated battle of sexes; Cooper et al. (1989) motivated their communication treatments precisely because miscoordination was common

game:beauty_contest_iterated.note: Ho, Camerer & Weigelt (1998, AER) on iterated p-beauty contests and Bosch-Domenech et al. (2002, AER) support convergence toward the Nash prediction with repetition, and the finding that executives are no more sophisticated than students initially. | k=12/N=2000 unsourced

game:beauty_contest_standard.note: Nagel (1995, AER) is correctly cited. 33 is the level-1 point for p = 2/3 (50p), not an observed mean: first-round means in lab pools are ~36-37 for p = 2/3 and ~27 for p = 1/2, i.e. above 50p and increasing in p. First-round SD is roughly 20 points of 100. Newspaper pools (Bosch-Domenech et al. 2002) average lower (~23) and are not what this standard entry describes. Recalled, not source-verified.

game:bertrand_competition_standard.note: Dufwenberg & Gneezy (2000, IJIO) 'Price competition and market concentration' found supracompetitive duopoly prices collapsing toward marginal cost with three or more firms - exactly the n_firms moderator pattern here. | k=15/N=1400 unsourced; Argenton & Muller's year/venue is uncertain to me

game:centipede_standard.note: McKelvey & Palfrey (1992, Econometrica) is the canonical centipede experiment - almost no one stops at the first node - and Levitt, List & Sadoff (2011, AER) extends it to chess players; the normalized DV is an aggregation the papers do not report. | k=15/N=1400 unsourced; The DV ('proportion of game played before stopping') is not directly comparable across the 4/6/10-move variants used in the cited studies

game:chicken_hawk_dove_standard.note: Rapoport & Chammah (1966) and Neugebauer, Poulsen & Schram (2008, JEBO) are real Chicken/Hawk-Dove studies and a roughly even Dove split is plausible; the dispersion field is incompatible with a binary DV. | A binary Dove/Hawk choice at p=0.52 has individual SD ~0.50, not 0.22; Rapoport & Chammah (1966) is a very early study; k=10/N=900 pooling is unsourced

game:common_pool_resource_standard.note: Over-extraction relative to the social optimum is the standard CPR lab result (Ostrom, Walker & Gardner 1992, APSR), but extraction/endowment ratios are design-specific. | Duplicates game:tragedy_of_commons_standard with a different mean (0.65 vs 0.62) and a different source; the two entries should not disagree; Ostrom, Gardner & Walker (1994) is a book; k=18/N=1800 unsourced

game:common_pool_resource_with_communica.note: Ostrom, Walker & Gardner (1992, APSR) 'Covenants with and without a sword' and Hackett, Schlager & Walker (1994, JEEM) both show communication substantially curbs over-extraction, with face-to-face strongest. | k=14/N=1200 unsourced

corrected.notes: Quantity relative to the Cournot-Nash quantity: duopolies produce BELOW Nash (partial collusion, ratio ~0.85-0.95), triopoly is near Nash, and four or more firms produce ABOVE Nash (ratio >1).
corrected.notes_was: Quantity/Nash equilibrium quantity ratio. Slight overproduction (above Nash). More competitive than theory.

game:cournot_competition_standard.note: Huck, Normann & Oechssler (2004, JEBO) 'Two are few and four are many' is the canonical number-effects result: duopoly collusive, four firms more competitive than Cournot. The ratio metric here is internally inconsistent. | A quantity/Nash ratio of 0.58 means massive underproduction, which contradicts the entry's own 'slight overproduction above Nash' note - the scale appears to be wrong; The n_firms ordering is directionally right (more firms -> more output) but the levels cannot be ratios to Nash

corrected.notes: Charity recipient roughly triples giving relative to an anonymous student recipient (Eckel & Grossman 1996: ~10.6% to ~31%).
corrected.notes_was: Charity as receiver increases mean giving ~50% above standard DG.

game:dictator_charity.note: Eckel & Grossman (1996, GEB) 'Altruism in anonymous dictator games' is the right source; their charity treatment gave ~31% versus ~11% to an anonymous counterpart. | 0.42 and '~50% above standard DG' understate the direction: Eckel & Grossman found a ~3x increase from a low baseline, landing near 0.31; 'Engel (2011) subset' is a vague provenance label

game:dictator_deserving_receiver.note: Ruffle (1998, GEB) studies earned desert in dictator/ultimatum games and Eckel & Grossman (1996, GEB) the charity recipient; both are real but the two entries are not cleanly separated. | Eckel & Grossman (1996) is the charity-recipient study and is also used for game:dictator_charity; the 'deserving receiver' and 'charity' entries overlap in sources but report different means (0.38 vs 0.42); charity_type moderator (Red Cross etc.) belongs to the charity entry, not a desert manipulation

game:dictator_earned_money.note: Cherry et al. (2002, AER) 'Hardnose the dictator' and Oxoby & Spraggon (2008, JEBO) are the right property-rights citations; the receiver-earned moderator direction (more giving) is also right, but the earned-endowment level is understated in magnitude. | Cherry, Frykblom & Shogren (2002) found ~95% gave zero and near-zero mean giving in the earned + double-blind condition; 0.15 with 55% zeros is far too generous; k=18/N=1600 unsourced

game:dictator_ingroup.note: Whitt & Wilson (2007, AJPS, postwar Bosnia) and Bernhard, Fischbacher & Fehr (2006, Nature, parochial altruism) are real and show ingroup favouritism in dictator allocations; magnitudes are study-specific. | k=22/N=2800 unsourced; neither cited paper is a meta-analysis; 'minimal' groups set at 0.32 vs ethnic/political ~0.37 asserts a minimal-vs-real-group ordering not established by these two studies

corrected.source: Andreoni (2007); Branas-Garza et al. (multiple-recipient dictator games)

game:dictator_multiple_recipients.note: Both citations are real papers but neither studies multiple-recipient dictator games; the per-recipient-dilution claim needs a different source (e.g. Andreoni 2007 on charitable giving to many recipients). | Andreoni & Bernheim (2009, Econometrica) is about the 50-50 norm and audience/social-image effects, not multiple recipients; Bolton & Ockenfels (2000, AER) is the ERC theory paper, not an experiment on recipient number

game:dictator_outgroup.note: Fershtman & Gneezy (2001, QJE) and Dimant (2024, Management Science, 'Hate Trumps Love') are real and do document outgroup discrimination in allocation games; the pooled numbers mix paradigms. | Iyengar & Westwood (2015) found strong partisan discrimination in the scholarship/implicit tasks but comparatively weak discrimination in their economic games - the entry leans on it for a dictator-game magnitude it does not strongly support; The d~0.6-0.9 polarization figure and the 0.20 dictator mean are from different literatures, pooled here without a common metric

game:dictator_social_distance.note: Hoffman, McCabe & Smith (1996, AER) and Bohnet & Frey (1999, AER comment) are the canonical social-distance pair and the monotone ordering is right; the double-blind anchor is too high. | Hoffman, McCabe & Smith (1996) report ~10% mean giving with ~64% zeros in their double-blind condition, not 0.22

game:dictator_standard.note: Engel (2011) dictator meta-study: mean 28.3%, bimodal at 0 and 0.5, ~36% selfish, ~17% equal split. Mean, modes, k and N all match; only the dispersion is understated. | sd_proportion=0.18 is too small for the stated distribution: 36% at zero plus 17% at half implies an individual-level SD of ~0.25; ci_95 of +/-0.03 is far wider than the sampling SE at N=20,813 (~0.002); it is a heterogeneity interval, not a CI

game:dictator_taking.note: List (2007, JPE) and Bardsley (2008, Exp Econ) both show the take option collapses apparent altruism; the subpopulation vector here is inconsistent with its own mean and with Engel's baseline. | The stated subpopulations imply a mean of ~0.20, not the stated 0.12; fair_divider=0.35 exceeds the equal-split share in the STANDARD dictator game (0.17), but adding a take option reduces fair splits rather than more than doubling them; List (2007)/Bardsley (2008) are single papers; k=12/N=1847 is an unsourced pooling

game:dictator_third_party_punishment.note: Fehr & Fischbacher (2004, Evolution and Human Behavior) is the right third-party punishment source and ~55-60% of third parties punishing matches it; the entry mixes the allocator and punisher DVs. | mean_proportion (0.25) is a dictator-giving number while the subpopulations and note describe observer punishment - two different DVs in one entry; k=8/N=800 unsourced

game:dictator_uncertainty.note: Dana, Weber & Kuang (2007, Economic Theory) 'Exploiting moral wiggle room' is correctly cited: hidden consequences cut fair choices roughly in half, consistent with the reduced giving here. | Larson & Capra (2009) is a critical comment reporting a weaker/order-dependent wiggle-room effect; the entry does not flag that qualification; k=12/N=1100 unsourced

game:die_roll_honesty.note: Abeler, Nosenzo & Raymond (2019, Econometrica) 'Preferences for truth-telling' meta-analyses ~90 studies and ~44,000 participants, and finds partial lying with a majority reporting truthfully - k, N and the subpopulation split match well. | The modal report in die-roll/coin-flip paradigms is the MAXIMUM payoff outcome, not 0.83; 'Mean reported ~58% of maximum' is at the low end; reported means in that literature usually run ~0.60-0.70 of maximum against a 0.50 truthful benchmark

game:first_price_auction_standard.note: Kagel & Levin's handbook survey documents robust overbidding above RNNE in first-price sealed-bid auctions; the single pooled ratio hides the bidder-number benchmark it must be compared against. | A bid/value ratio of 0.82 is only 'overbidding' relative to the n-specific RNNE benchmark; stated without n it is uninterpretable (RNNE is 0.50 at n=2, 0.90 at n=10)

game:gift_exchange_standard.note: Fehr, Kirchsteiger & Riedl (1993, QJE) established the wage-effort reciprocity relation; the pooled effort level is not comparable across the normalizations used in that literature. | mean_proportion=0.45 for 'effort' is scale-dependent (effort is normalized differently across gift-exchange designs) and is not a figure Fehr et al. (1993) report

game:holt_laury_standard.note: Holt & Laury (2002, AER): subjects are modestly risk averse at low real stakes and more so as stakes scale; the mean here is slightly high and the spread too tight. | Holt & Laury's low-real-stakes mean is ~5.2 safe choices, so 5.8/10 is at the high end; sd_proportion=0.12 implies SD ~1.2 safe choices; the observed dispersion is nearer 1.8

game:market_entry_standard.note: Sundali, Rapoport & Seale (1995, OBHDP) and Rapoport, Seale & Winter (2002, GEB) document the striking aggregate convergence to the equilibrium entry rate, which the capacity moderator captures better than the headline mean. | A single pooled entry rate of 0.55 is uninformative because the central result is that entry TRACKS capacity; the entry rate is near c by construction; k=14/N=1600 unsourced

game:mini_ultimatum.note: Falk, Fehr & Fischbacher (2003, Economic Inquiry) 'On the nature of fair behavior' is exactly the mini-ultimatum choice-set design showing intention-based fairness, and Guth, Huck & Muller (2001, GEB) is the right companion on equal splits. | k=12/N=1400 unsourced

game:nash_bargaining_standard.note: The 50-50 focal outcome in unstructured bargaining is a real regularity surveyed by Roth (1995), but the SD and CI here are not quantities that survey reports. | Roth (1995) is a handbook survey; k=30/N=3000 is unsourced

game:prisoners_dilemma_asymmetric.note: The symmetric/asymmetric PD comparison and the inequity-aversion interpretation are a real line of work, but the specific author-year pairs here are ones I can only half-place. | I cannot place 'Ahn et al. (2007)' precisely; the Ahn/Ostrom/Schmidt/Walker PD work I recall is 2001 (Public Choice) on fear, greed and history of play; Beckenkamp, Hennig-Schmidt & Maier-Rigaud (2007) is a working paper, a weak calibration source

game:prisoners_dilemma_costly_signaling.note: Both citations are real but neither is a costly-signalling prisoner's dilemma experiment, and the subpopulation vector contradicts the entry's own mean. | Gintis, Smith & Bowles (2001, J Theoretical Biology) is a formal costly-signalling model, not an experiment; Smith & Bliege Bird (2000, Evolution and Human Behavior) is ethnographic fieldwork on turtle hunting and feast-giving, not a lab prisoner's dilemma; The subpopulations imply total cooperation of 0.70 (0.50 signaller-cooperators + 0.20 non-signaller-cooperators), inconsistent with mean_proportion=0.58

game:prisoners_dilemma_exit_option.note: Orbell & Dawes (1993, Am Sociological Review) 'the option of not playing the game' is the right experimental source for exit options and cooperators' advantage via assortment; the companion citation is theoretical. | Batali & Kitcher (1995, J Theoretical Biology) is an evolutionary simulation, not an experiment, so it cannot support behavioural proportions; k=10/N=1200 unsourced

corrected.source: Dal Bo & Frechette (2011); Dal Bo & Frechette (2018 survey)

game:prisoners_dilemma_iterated_axelrod.note: Dal Bo & Frechette (2011, AER) 'The evolution of cooperation in infinitely repeated games' is the right empirical anchor; Axelrod supplies theory, not data. | Axelrod (1984) is a computer-tournament/evolutionary monograph, not a human experiment, and should not anchor human cooperation rates; Dal Bo & Frechette (2011, AER) found cooperation rates that were often low (frequently 10-40%) and highly sensitive to delta and payoffs; a pooled 60% is too high; The round_block moderator rises over time, but increases with experience occur only when cooperation is both an equilibrium and risk dominant

game:prisoners_dilemma_multiplayer.note: Both citations are real group-size cooperation studies; the clean monotone decline from 0.50 (3 players) to 0.28 (20+) is stronger than that literature supports. | Barcelo & Capraro (2015, Scientific Reports) report that group-size effects on one-shot cooperation are not uniformly negative across dilemmas, so the monotone decline asserted here is contested; Grujic et al. (2010, PLoS ONE) is a spatial/lattice PD design, a poor match for an N-player one-shot calibration

game:prisoners_dilemma_standard.note: Sally (1995, Rationality and Society) gives mean cooperation ~47% across PD experiments; modes at 0/1 are right but the SD is incompatible with a Bernoulli DV. | Cooperation in a one-shot PD is a binary choice, so the individual-level SD at p=0.47 is ~0.50, not 0.20 (0.20 would be a between-study SD); n_participants=26000 is a round figure not reported by Sally | SECOND PASS (2026-10-08): a Bernoulli(0.47) has SD 0.5, which no Beta can match, so on a 0-100 slider the entry fell back to a generic tendency (63-70% cooperation); the two point masses state the bimodality explicitly

corrected.notes: Punishment opportunities raise cooperation, but costly punishment often fails to raise group payoffs and the highest earners punish least (Dreber et al. 2008); antisocial punishment can erase the gain.
corrected.notes_was: Punishment increases cooperation ~23%. But costly punishment can reduce group payoffs.

game:prisoners_dilemma_with_punishment.note: Both citations are real (Rand et al. 2009, Science) but Dreber et al.'s headline is that costly punishment does not improve payoffs, which the entry's framing inverts. | Dreber, Rand, Fudenberg & Nowak (2008, Nature) is titled 'Winners don't punish' and is evidence AGAINST punishment paying - citing it for a '+23% cooperation' benefit misrepresents it

game:prisoners_dilemma_with_reputation.note: Both citations are real and the indirect-reciprocity/image-scoring mechanism is correctly described, but the paradigm label (prisoner's dilemma) does not match either source. | Milinski, Semmann & Krambeck (2002, Nature) used an indirect-reciprocity giving/public-goods design with image scoring, not a prisoner's dilemma; Nowak & Sigmund (2005, Nature) is a theory review and supplies no behavioural levels

game:public_goods_peer_punishment.note: Fehr & Gachter (2002, Nature) 'Altruistic punishment in humans' plus Nikiforakis & Normann (2008, Exp Econ) support both the sustained high contributions and the punishment-effectiveness-ratio moderator (more effective punishment -> higher contributions). | The 'antisocial punishment ~15%' figure is from Herrmann, Thoni & Gachter (2008, Science), which is not cited

game:public_goods_repeated_decay.note: Isaac, Walker & Williams (1994, JPubE) 'Group size and the voluntary provision of public goods' is the standard refutation of a simple negative group-size effect; the round-block decay figures are the classic Ledyard (1995) pattern and look right. | The group_size moderator declines with size (4:0.40 -> 40:0.25), but Isaac, Walker & Williams (1994) - the cited paper - famously found NO decline and sometimes higher contributions in large groups once MPCR is held constant

game:public_goods_standard.note: Zelmer (2003, Exp Econ) linear public-goods meta-analysis; the MPCR and punishment moderator directions match but the headline level is the un-decayed first-round number. | 0.47 pools one-shot/first-round contributions with repeated-game averages; Zelmer (2003) pooled mean is ~0.38 and round-10 levels are 0.10-0.20; distribution_shape 'right_skew' with mode 0.5 is internally odd; VCM contributions are typically bimodal at 0 and full | SECOND PASS (2026-10-08): one-shot / first-round contributions are spread over the whole endowment (SD about 0.30 of it); 0.18 could not hold the zero and full-contribution clusters the first audit noted

corrected.source: Van de Kragt, Orbell & Dawes (1983); Rapoport & Eshed-Levy (1989)
corrected.source_was: Van de Kragt et al. (1986); Rapoport & Eshed-Levy (1989)

game:public_goods_step_level.note: Rapoport & Eshed-Levy (1989, OBHDP) on greed and fear in step-level public goods is correctly cited; the all-or-nothing bimodality and large-group coordination failure match that literature. | The canonical minimal-contributing-set paper is Van de Kragt, Orbell & Dawes (1983, APSR), not 1986

game:public_goods_threshold.note: Croson & Marks (2000, Exp Econ) is itself a meta- and experimental analysis of step returns in threshold public goods, and Cadsby & Maynes (1999, JPubE) supports the refund-rule and bimodal-contribution pattern. | k=18/N=1800 may not match Croson & Marks's published counts

game:public_goods_with_communication.note: Isaac & Walker (1988, Economic Inquiry) and Bochet, Page & Putterman (2006, JEBO) support both the overall level and the moderator ordering: face-to-face strongest, numerical signals largely ineffective. | k=22/N=2500 unsourced

game:public_goods_with_inequality.note: Cherry, Kroll & Shogren (2005, JEBO) and Chan et al. (1999, Exp Econ) are real; the 'low-endowment subjects contribute a larger proportion' pattern matches Chan et al., but the aggregate claim is contested. | Chan, Mestelman, Moir & Muller (1999) found heterogeneity could RAISE total contributions in some parameterizations, so 'inequality reduces total contributions' is stated too flatly; k=12/N=1200 unsourced

game:public_goods_with_leadership.note: Guth, Levati, Sutter & van der Heijden (2007, JPubE) and Levati, Sutter & van der Heijden (2007) are real leading-by-example studies; the appointed/elected contrast is imported from elsewhere. | 'Elected leaders most effective' is not a result of either cited paper; that comes from the later endogenous-institution literature (e.g. Sutter, Haigner & Kocher 2010); k=10/N=1000 unsourced

game:public_goods_with_punishment.note: Fehr & Gachter (2000, AER) 'Cooperation and punishment in public goods experiments' does show contributions rising toward 80-90% of endowment with punishment, but only after several rounds. | ~0.80 is the LATE-round level under punishment in Fehr & Gachter (2000); the sequence average is lower (~0.55-0.70); k=15/N=1500 unsourced

corrected.notes: Rewards raise contributions relative to no institution; whether they are weaker than punishment is contested - Rand et al. (2009) find reward at least as effective once payoffs rather than contributions are the criterion.
corrected.notes_was: Rewards less effective than punishment for sustaining cooperation. +13% above baseline.

norm:technology_anxiety_ta.note: Meuter, Ostrom, Bitner & Roundtree (2003, Journal of Business Research) on technology anxiety and Parasuraman (2000, Journal of Service Research) TRI are both real 5-point instruments; a below-midpoint mean rising with age is the established pattern. | 'TRI-TA' is a constructed label: Parasuraman's TRI has discomfort and insecurity dimensions, not a subscale named technology anxiety

norm:test_anxiety_rta.note: Benson & El-Zahhar (1994) validated the RTA on a 4-point format; a worry-subscale mean ~2.3 with higher female scores is the standard finding in the test-anxiety literature. | The scale is the Revised Test Anxiety scale (RTA); 'RTT' appears to be a typo

norm:test_anxiety_tai.note: Spielberger's Test Anxiety Inventory (1980) is 4-point 'almost never'-'almost always', 20 items; Chapell et al. (2005, JEP) is a real large-N undergraduate/graduate study. Per-item ~2.0-2.2 and higher female scores are standard.

norm:tolerance_of_ambiguity.note: Budner (1962, J Pers) and McLain (2009, Psychol Rep, MSTAT-II) are both real, but I cannot place a published MSTAT-II mean, and the two sources point in opposite scoring directions. | Budner (1962) is a 16-item 7-point scale and McLain's MSTAT-II is a 13-item 5-point scale; with scale_name='MSTAT-II' and scale_points=5 the Budner citation is on the wrong metric; Budner's scale is scored for INtolerance, the opposite pole of the stated construct

norm:trait_anger_staxi2.note: STAXI-2 (Spielberger 1999) Trait Anger is 10 items on a 1-4 format; normative totals ~17-18 give a per-item mean near 1.75 with strong positive skew, and gender differences in trait anger are small — all as stated.

norm:trait_curiosity_cei.note: CEI-II (Kashdan et al. 2009, Journal of Research in Personality) is 10 items on a 5-point format with means ~3.5-3.8 and SD ~0.65-0.75, matching the entry.

norm:trust_in_others_gts.note: Yamagishi & Yamagishi's (1994, Motivation and Emotion) General Trust Scale is a 5-point agreement measure, and their core finding is lower general trust in Japan than the US — matching the east_asian < western < scandinavian ordering. Naef & Schupp (2009) is the real SOEP trust paper.

norm:turnover_intention_tis.note: TIS-6 (Bothma & Roodt 2013, SA Journal of Human Resource Management) is a 6-item 5-point measure; a mean below the midpoint with mild positive skew is the standard pattern.

norm:vitality_svs.note: Ryan & Frederick (1997, J Pers) is the Subjective Vitality Scale on a 7-point scale, with means around 4.5-5.0 and SD ~1.1-1.3 in unselected samples. | the SVS exists as a 7-item and a 6-item version; the entry does not say which

norm:wom_intention_wom.note: Both citations are real (Journal of Marketing 1996; Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences 2010) and 7-point is the right format, but mean 4.3 / SD 1.4 is context-dependent. | Zeithaml, Berry & Parasuraman (1996) report WOM intentions for specific service firms, and Goyette et al. (2010) is an eWOM scale-development paper; neither gives a general-population norm

norm:work_engagement_uwes.note: UWES-9 (Schaufeli, Bakker & Salanova 2006, EPM) uses a 0-6 frequency scale (7 options) and the 2003 manual reports total means around 3.8-4.0 with SD ~1.1. The rise with age is in the manual's norm tables. | SECOND PASS (2026-10-08): the instrument is scored from zero and the stored mean is on that native metric, but scale_min was left at the default 1.0, so the rescale to a 1-7 item put the mean one scale point too low (see get_construct_norm)

norm:work_family_conflict_wfc.note: Netemeyer, Boles & McMurrian (1996, JAP) WFC is 5 items on a 7-point format with means ~3.3-3.9 and SD ~1.3, consistent with the entry. | The female-higher WFC moderator is weakly supported: meta-analyses (e.g. Byron 2005) find gender differences in work-to-family conflict close to zero

norm:workplace_incivility_wis.note: Cortina, Magley, Williams & Langhout (2001, JOHP) is the right source, the 0-4 frequency format gives 5 options, and a low mean (~0.7-0.9) with strong positive skew plus higher female exposure matches their findings. | Cortina et al. (2001) introduced a 7-item WIS; the 12-item version comes from Cortina et al. (2013); sample_type 'general' should be an employed sample

norm:worry_pswq.note: Meyer, Miller, Metzger & Borkovec (1990, Behav Res Ther) developed the 16-item PSWQ on a 5-point scale; non-clinical totals ~43-48 (~2.7-3.0/item) and GAD-patient totals ~62-68 (~3.9-4.25/item) match the entry's base mean and moderators, as does women>men.

order:carryover_effect.note: Schuman & Presser (1981) and Tourangeau, Rips & Rasinski (2000) are the right literature for context effects, and Schwarz & Strack's assimilation/contrast account is the mechanism; the numeric shape is invented. | magnitude_per_item = 0.1 as a correlation increment over trait correlation, with a 3-item decay window, is an engineering parameterization; neither cited source reports such a coefficient; Schuman & Presser (1981) document specific question-order experiments (e.g. the general/specific abortion and communist-reporter items) whose shifts are percentage-point changes in marginals, not inflated inter-item correlations

order:primacy_effect.note: Krosnick & Alwin (1987, POQ) is correct for response-order effects and the note's claim (visually presented lists favor early options) is their finding; the 0.05 magnitude is not theirs. | magnitude_per_item = 0.05 is an engineering parameter, not a published effect size; Krosnick & Alwin report shifts in option-choice proportions, not a scale-point shift; onset_item = plateau_item = 1 makes the fields vestigial here — primacy is a within-item response-order effect, not a position-in-questionnaire effect, so this row reuses a schema built for fatigue curves

order:recency_effect.note: The note is faithful to Krosnick & Alwin (1987) and Krosnick (1991) satisficing theory: recency dominates for aurally presented or long lists, primacy for visual/written presentation. Only the magnitude is invented. | magnitude_per_item = 0.04 is an engineering parameter with no published counterpart; Same schema mismatch as the primacy row: onset/plateau at item 1 are inert fields

order:straight_lining_acceleration.note: Zhang & Conrad (2014, Survey Research Methods) links speeding to straightlining, and Kim, Dykema, Stevenson, Black & Moberg (2019, Social Science Computer Review 37(2), 214-233) is a real straightlining-measurement paper; the increasing-with-length direction is sound, the parameters are not published. | magnitude_per_item = 0.005, onset_item = 30 and plateau_item = 100 are an engineering parameterization; neither paper reports a per-item straightlining hazard rate or a knee at item 30; Kim et al. (2019) is primarily about how straightlining is MEASURED (comparing indicators) and its mode differences, so attaching a length-acceleration coefficient to it overreaches

order:survey_fatigue.note: Galesic & Bosnjak (2009, POQ) and Hoerger (2010, Cyberpsychology) are real and the qualitative claims (later items get faster, shorter, more midpoint-ish) match them plus Herzog & Bachman (1981) response-set fatigue; the three shape parameters are invented. | magnitude_per_item = -0.003, onset_item = 20 and plateau_item = 80 are an engineering parameterization of the fatigue curve, not published quantities; neither cited paper reports a per-item degradation rate or a knee at item 20; Galesic & Bosnjak (2009) manipulated stated questionnaire LENGTH and measured participation, break-off and quality indicators by question position; Hoerger (2010) is about dropout as a function of length, not mean/variance drift

order:survey_learning.note: Knowles (1988, JPSP, 'Item context effects on personality scales: measuring changes the measure') is the apt citation — later items in a scale correlate better with the total — and Tourangeau, Rips & Rasinski (2000) is the standard survey-response text. Direction right, parameters invented. | magnitude_per_item = 0.002, onset_item = 1, plateau_item = 15 are an engineering parameterization; Knowles reports increasing item-total correlations with serial position but not a per-item variance-reduction coefficient or a 15-item plateau

rt:iat_trial_congruent.note: Greenwald, Nosek & Banaji (2003, JPSP) 'Understanding and using the IAT: I. An improved scoring algorithm' is the right citation and the D-score definition in the note is correct; the absolute latency is on the fast side of what I recall for web IAT samples. | 650 ms is at the fast end; congruent-block means in typical IAT datasets run roughly 750-900 ms, with the scoring algorithm's 300 ms / 10,000 ms trimming bounds implying a broader spread; sd_ms 150 vs the ex-Gaussian implication sqrt(80^2 + 100^2) = 128 ms is a modest (~17%) inconsistency; the mean identity mu + tau = 650 holds

rt:iat_trial_incongruent.note: With these two rows the implied D = 150 ms over a pooled SD of ~200-300 ms gives D ~0.5-0.75, which is in line with published race/age IAT effect magnitudes, so the paired values hang together even if the absolute levels are fast. | 800 ms is fast for an incongruent block (typical means run ~900-1100 ms), though the ~150 ms congruency difference is the more consequential quantity and is in a defensible range; sd_ms 200 vs the ex-Gaussian implication sqrt(100^2 + 120^2) = 156 ms is a ~28% inconsistency; mean identity mu + tau = 800 holds

rt:likert_careless.note: Meade & Craig (2012, Psychological Methods) is real and about careless responding, but the per-item millisecond values are not from it; the ex-Gaussian SD is also arithmetically wrong. | Ex-Gaussian internal inconsistency: SD = sqrt(150^2 + 150^2) = 212 ms, not 300 ms. Mean identity mu + tau = 600 holds.; Meade & Craig (2012) identify careless responding via response-pattern and factor-mixture indices; they do not publish a 600 ms per-item latency norm. The usual latency anchor is Huang et al. (2012), who flag responding faster than ~2 s per item.; A 600 ms mean per Likert item is faster than typical careless-responding cutoffs and is near simple-RT floor

rt:likert_engaged.note: Yan & Tourangeau (2008, Applied Cognitive Psychology, 'Fast times and easy questions') is real and 3-5 s per Likert item is consistent with web paradata norms; only the SD is arithmetically off given the stated ex-Gaussian parameters. | Ex-Gaussian internal inconsistency: SD = sqrt(sigma^2 + tau^2) = sqrt(600^2 + 800^2) = 1000 ms, not 1200 ms. The mean identity (mu + tau = 3200 + 800 = 4000) does hold.; Yan & Tourangeau (2008) report item-level web-survey latencies by age and question complexity but not this specific mu/sigma/tau decomposition, which is an engineering parameterization

rt:likert_satisficing.note: Citation real and the direction (satisficers roughly 2-3x faster than engaged respondents) matches the speeding literature; the stated SD contradicts the stated ex-Gaussian parameters. | Ex-Gaussian internal inconsistency: SD = sqrt(300^2 + 300^2) = 424 ms, not 600 ms (a 41% overstatement). Mean identity mu + tau = 1500 holds.; The 1500 ms satisficing mean is a plausible engineering value but not a number Yan & Tourangeau publish as a satisficing norm

rt:open_ended_careless.note: A ~2 s open-ended latency is a reasonable stand-in for a one-word or junk answer, but it is not a quantity from Meade & Craig (2012, Psychological Methods) or any OE-timing norm I can name. | Meade & Craig (2012) does not report open-ended response latencies; its indices are pattern-based (long-string, even-odd consistency, Mahalanobis D) plus self-report diligence items; mean_ms 2000 / sd_ms 1000 are engineering parameters

rt:open_ended_engaged.note: The citation is real but about a different measure; 20-45 s for a considered open-ended answer is reasonable on its face, yet I know of no published distributional norm supporting these exact values. | Zhang & Conrad (2014, Survey Research Methods) is about speeding and its association with straightlining on grid/closed items; it is not a source for open-ended composition-time norms; mean_ms 35000 / sd_ms 15000 and the '20-45s' note are plausible engineering values but I cannot attribute them to any published paradata norm

rt:open_ended_satisficing.note: Direction (satisficers roughly 6x faster on open-ended items) is plausible and consistent with the speeding literature, but the cited paper does not supply open-ended timing and the numbers are unplaceable. | Same citation mismatch as the engaged row: Zhang & Conrad (2014) measures speeding on closed items, not open-ended response durations; mean_ms 6000 / sd_ms 3000 are engineering parameters with no published counterpart I can identify

rt:slider_engaged.note: Funke, Reips & Thomas (2011, Social Science Computer Review 29, 221-231, 'Sliders for the smart') confirms sliders are slower than radio buttons, so the direction is right; the specific parameters are an engineering parameterization and the SD is arithmetically off. | Ex-Gaussian internal inconsistency: SD = sqrt(800^2 + 1300^2) = 1526 ms, not 1800 ms. Mean identity mu + tau = 5500 holds.; Funke, Reips & Thomas (2011) report substantially higher response times (and ~7x break-off odds) for slider scales but do not publish a 5500 ms mean or an ex-Gaussian decomposition

rt:slider_satisficing.note: Funke, Reips & Thomas (2011) is a real and apt slider-timing citation and a lognormal RT shape is standard (Ratcliff; Luce), but these particular numbers I cannot place in the literature. | mean_ms 2500 / sd_ms 800 are engineering parameters, not values Funke et al. (2011) report; distribution is 'lognormal' while mean/sd are given on the raw ms scale with the ex-Gaussian fields zeroed; the lognormal mu/sigma are never specified, so the row cannot be instantiated from its own fields without an implicit moment-matching step
